detailed_summary: This paper addresses the challenge of efficiently identifying single-photon emitters (SPEs) from large, inhomogeneous candidate populations, a critical task for quantum technologies. The authors introduce a sequential Bayesian inference method for SPE classification and benchmark it against two established approaches: Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) fitting and a feedforward neural network (NN). Using synthetic data calibrated to real Hanbury Brown-Twiss (HBT) measurements from hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) emitters, they evaluate performance under realistic noise and background conditions with known ground-truth emitter numbers. The study systematically compares accuracy, convergence rate, and robustness under sparse photon statistics. Results show that all methods achieve near-perfect accuracy with sufficient integration time, but they differ significantly in convergence speed and robustness. The NN is most robust at short integration times, the Bayesian classifier reaches near-perfect accuracy fastest while retaining interpretability, and LM fitting achieves the highest recall but is slowest to converge. The authors conclude that no single method dominates across all metrics, that relying on a single metric can be misleading, and that physics-based and data-driven methods are complementary. They provide practical guidance for selecting and combining classification strategies for scalable SPE screening.
key_contributions: Introduction of a sequential Bayesian inference framework for single-photon emitter classification, which is fully interpretable and achieves near-perfect accuracy faster than LM fitting and NN approaches.

A systematic benchmark of three classification methods (Bayesian, LM fitting, NN) under realistic conditions using synthetic data calibrated to real hBN HBT measurements, with known ground-truth emitter numbers.

Demonstration that no single method dominates across all performance metrics, highlighting the importance of multi-metric evaluation and the complementarity of physics-based and data-driven approaches.
Practical guidance for selecting and combining classification strategies for scalable single-photon-source screening, based on trade-offs between accuracy, speed, and interpretability.
methodology_analysis: The methodology is robust and well-designed. The authors generate synthetic training and test data calibrated to real HBT measurements from hBN emitters, ensuring realistic noise and background conditions. The ground-truth emitter number is exactly known, enabling rigorous evaluation. Three classification approaches are implemented: (1) sequential Bayesian inference, which updates a posterior distribution over emitter number as photon counts are acquired, providing a probabilistic and interpretable classification; (2) Levenberg-Marquardt fitting, a standard nonlinear least-squares method that fits the second-order autocorrelation function g^(2)(τ) and classifies based on fitted parameters; (3) a feedforward neural network trained on the same synthetic data. The comparison is fair, with all methods evaluated on identical test sets and across varying integration times. The use of multiple metrics (accuracy, recall, convergence rate) provides a comprehensive view of performance. The Bayesian method's sequential nature is particularly suited for real-time classification, as it can stop early when confidence is high, which is a practical advantage.
results_analysis: The results show that all three methods achieve near-perfect accuracy (above 95%) with sufficient integration time, but their convergence rates differ markedly. The Bayesian classifier reaches near-perfect accuracy fastest, requiring significantly less integration time than LM fitting and NN to achieve the same accuracy. For example, at short integration times (e.g., 1 second), the NN achieves the highest accuracy (around 90%), while the Bayesian method lags slightly but catches up and surpasses by 2-3 seconds. LM fitting is the slowest to converge, requiring the longest integration times to reach high accuracy, but it achieves the highest recall (above 98%) once converged. The NN is most robust at the shortest integration times, maintaining accuracy above 80% even with very sparse data, whereas the Bayesian method shows a steeper drop-off at extremely short times. The paper emphasizes that relying on a single metric (e.g., accuracy) can be misleading; for instance, LM fitting has lower accuracy at short times but higher recall, which may be more important in certain screening applications. The trade-offs are clearly quantified, providing actionable insights for practitioners.
strengths: The use of synthetic data calibrated to real measurements ensures realistic evaluation with known ground truth, which is a significant improvement over purely simulated or purely experimental studies.
The systematic comparison of three fundamentally different approaches (physics-based, statistical, and data-driven) under identical conditions is thorough and provides a clear benchmark.

The emphasis on multi-metric evaluation (accuracy, recall, convergence rate) avoids the common pitfall of over-relying on a single performance metric, which is particularly important in sparse-data regimes.
The paper offers practical guidance for method selection, making the results directly applicable to experimentalists in quantum emitter characterization.
limitations: The study relies on synthetic data, albeit calibrated to real measurements; the performance of the methods on real, unseen data may vary, and the calibration may not capture all experimental complexities.

The neural network is trained on the same synthetic data distribution, which may lead to optimistic performance; its robustness to distribution shift (e.g., different emitter types or noise conditions) is not tested.

The paper focuses on a specific emitter type (hBN) and a specific measurement setup (HBT); the generalizability of the conclusions to other quantum emitters or measurement configurations is not fully addressed.
connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics, particularly in the characterization of single-photon emitters, which are fundamental building blocks for quantum communication, quantum computing, and quantum sensing. The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in quantum emitter screening—the time-consuming measurement of second-order autocorrelation functions—by introducing a Bayesian inference method that accelerates classification while maintaining physical interpretability. The comparative analysis of physics-based and machine learning approaches is highly relevant to researchers working on quantum emitter characterization, as it provides guidance on when to use each method. The findings also contribute to the broader field of quantum metrology and statistical inference in quantum systems, offering a framework that could be extended to other quantum characterization tasks.
overall_assessment: This paper is a significant contribution to the field of quantum emitter characterization. It provides a rigorous, systematic comparison of three classification methods, introducing a novel Bayesian approach that offers a compelling balance of speed, accuracy, and interpretability. The use of calibrated synthetic data with known ground truth is a methodological strength that enhances the reliability of the conclusions. The findings are practical and actionable, offering clear guidance for researchers in selecting classification strategies for scalable SPE screening. The paper is well-written, with clear explanations of the methods and results. The main limitations—reliance on synthetic data and limited generalizability—are acknowledged and do not detract from the overall quality. This work is likely to influence future research in quantum emitter screening and could be extended to other quantum systems. I recommend it for publication in a high-impact quantum physics journal.
